name: Carla Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking to me, Carla. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group that isn't linked to any company, union, party or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can share what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What's a normal working day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Hollins Roofing and Joinery, a firm of six out in the countryside. We do new timber roofs, barn conversions, that kind of thing. I'm up on the scaffold fixing battens, the thin strips of wood the tiles hang on, rolling out the membrane, carrying trusses with the lads, and painting fascia boards. I'm fifty-eight and the junior, because I came to it late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up roofing?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We had a dairy farm, my husband Karl and me, for nearly thirty years. Milk prices killed it, and we sold the herd and most of the land in 2019 to clear the debts. I'd fixed every shed roof on that farm, so when old Mr Hollins needed a labourer, I asked. Karl drives a milk tanker now, so he still sees the cows, just from the road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love being up high on a clear morning, you can see three villages and the church spire. I like that it's honest work, you can see if you did it right. What wears me out is the wind in winter, and the young lads, who are kind, but treat me like their mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you are, the clever people got it wrong again. You still need someone on the roof. I'd say it at the choir practice tea and to Mr Hollins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the plan holds: work till sixty-five or so, then help Anna with the grandchildren. I'd be pleased, I don't need the world turned upside down twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working, keep putting a bit by, we've got about two months saved after the farm debts. Maybe go on the roofing course Mr Hollins mentioned, so I'm not just the labourer. My granddaughter Mia showed me the AI on my phone, and I'd keep using it for the odd question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled. Like the cows going in for milking at the right time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What sort of odd questions do you ask it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What roof pitch you need for slate, I asked it last month to check I'd understood. And recipes, if I'm honest, more recipes than roofs. Mia thinks it's hilarious that Granny uses it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't need the world turned upside down twice. What was the first time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selling the herd. Karl cried in the milking parlour, the only time I've seen him cry. I don't want another day like that.

S0.say: I'd say the clever people got it wrong again and you still need someone on the roof. I'd say it over tea at choir practice and to Mr Hollins.
S0.think: Privately it means the plan holds: work until about sixty-five, then help Anna with the grandchildren. I don't need the world turned upside down twice.
S0.do: Keeps working at Hollins and adding to about two months of savings left after the farm debts. Considers the roofing course and keeps using the phone AI for the odd question.
S0.feel: Calm and settled, like cows going in for milking on time.
S0.quote: Karl cried in the milking parlour, the only time I've seen him cry.
S0.fieldNote: Carla is a former dairy farmer for whom losing the farm was the big upheaval of her life. She uses AI casually, more for recipes than roofs. Her plans centre on family and finishing work on her own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should learn a trade properly, with apprenticeships, and not rely on computers to think for them. And I'd say firms like Mr Hollins's should be left alone to get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd worry a bit. Out here there aren't many building jobs, maybe three firms in the valley. If roofs start coming pre-made from a factory, like I hear some houses do, the labouring goes first, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the roofing course this year so I'm a proper roofer, not a labourer. I'd ask Mr Hollins's son, who does the quotes, whether there's anything with drones or computers I could help with, once I'd seen it work for other firms. And I'd keep saving, a little more if I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a cow off her food, nothing wrong yet, but you watch her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at Hollins you'd worry about more than yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Mr Hollins himself. He's seventy and won't retire, and if things change fast he'd find it hard. The son, Robert, is all tablets and drones already, he'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms should be left alone. Would you want any help from the government?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For apprenticeships, yes, that's money well spent. Not for paying people to sit at home. My dad would turn in his grave.

S1.say: I'd say people should learn a trade properly through apprenticeships and not let computers think for them. Firms like Mr Hollins's should be left alone to get on with it.
S1.think: Privately I'd worry a bit, because there are only about three building firms in the valley. If roofs come pre-made from factories, the labouring goes first, and that's me.
S1.do: Takes the roofing course this year to become a proper roofer, and asks the boss's son about drone or computer work once proven at other firms. Keeps saving a little more where possible.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a cow off her food that you keep watching.
S1.quote: Like a cow off her food, nothing wrong yet, but you watch her.
S1.fieldNote: Her farming language runs through everything she says. She'd move up from labourer and try new tools once other firms prove them, which fits her steady nature. She supports apprenticeship funding but not paying people to stay home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to look after our own communities, our villages, because nobody in the city will. The church and the families will have to hold things together. I'd say that at choir and in the village shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it would frighten me badly. I'd be sixty, and Karl's tanker would drive itself, they're already testing that sort of lorry. Two months of savings, both of us out, and three building firms in the valley all bringing in robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cut right back: sell Karl's old pickup, no holiday, nothing new. I'd get the hens going again and sell eggs and jam at the Saturday market, I know how to do that from the farm. And we'd have to ask the children for help, which I'd hate, and the church does a food bank, I'd swallow my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and ashamed at the same time. Losing sleep, like the year we sold the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Karl that first night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we did it once, we can do it again. He'd say we were forty then. And he'd be right, which is the worst part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather not take handouts. But you'd use the food bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, it doesn't add up. The church is neighbours helping neighbours, that feels different to the government. But if it came to it, I'd take whatever kept the house warm.

S2.say: I'd say we must look after our own villages because nobody in the city will. The church and families will have to hold things together, as I'd say at choir and the village shop.
S2.think: Privately it would frighten me badly: sixty, Karl's tanker driving itself, two months of savings and all three building firms in the valley bringing in robots.
S2.do: Sells Karl's old pickup and cuts holidays and purchases straight away. Restarts hens to sell eggs and jam at the Saturday market, and reluctantly asks her children and the church food bank for help.
S2.feel: Scared and ashamed, losing sleep like the year they sold the herd.
S2.quote: I'd say we did it once, we can do it again. He'd say we were forty then.
S2.fieldNote: Thin savings, a rural valley with few jobs and her husband's exposed driving job combine to alarm her. She noticed her own contradiction about handouts and admitted it. Her fallback is old farm skills, eggs and jam, rather than anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so get ready: pay off what you owe, help your kids learn something useful. I'd say it to my own children first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is better. I'd be sixty-three, and Karl and I could stop a couple of years early if we've saved and have the eggs and a bit of land rent coming in. It would be a squeeze, but not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting more aside now, a hundred extra a month, and get the hens going this spring instead of waiting. I'd do the roofing course to stay useful. And we'd plan to stop work at sixty-three, not sixty-six.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see the road. Like knowing a hard winter is coming and filling the barn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned land rent. Do you still have some land?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Six acres we kept behind the house. A neighbour grazes his sheep on it for a small rent. Not much, but it's something, and it's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Thomas, who works in a bank?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him the bank is the first place they'll use these machines. He'd say he knows, Mum. I'd tell him to come home and learn roofing, half joking.

S3.say: I'd say five years is time to get ready, so pay off what you owe and help your kids learn something useful. I'd say it to my own children first.
S3.think: Privately five years is better. At sixty-three, Karl and I could stop early with savings, eggs and a little land rent coming in, a squeeze but not a disaster.
S3.do: Saves an extra hundred a month and starts the hens this spring rather than later. Takes the roofing course to stay useful, and plans with Karl to stop at sixty-three instead of sixty-six.
S3.feel: Anxious but able to see the road, like filling the barn before a hard winter.
S3.quote: Like knowing a hard winter is coming and filling the barn.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her room to prepare in ways she trusts: savings, hens and the six acres. She's openly worried for her son in banking. The farm remains her mental toolbox for every plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and families should use it well. Teach the young ones a trade, keep the church and the village going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be sixty-eight and finished, so I'd be all right. My worry would be the village, whether there's any work at all for the young ones in the valley. And for Thomas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with Hollins until sixty-five, save steadily, and keep the hens as a hobby. I'd help pay for my grandchildren's apprenticeships when the time comes, if they want them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the village and the grandchildren, but not for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the village look like to you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worry it'd be quiet, all the young ones gone to the city. No one on the roofs, no one in the milking parlours. It's already half that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use the AI for the odd question. With ten years, would you learn more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, once everyone else had. Mia will drag me along. I'm not proud, just slow.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is fair warning and families should use it well. Teach young people a trade and keep the church and village going.
S4.think: Privately I'd be sixty-eight and finished, so I'd be all right. My worry would be whether there's any work for young people in the valley, and for my son Thomas.
S4.do: Carries on at Hollins until sixty-five, saves steadily and keeps hens as a hobby. Plans to help pay for her grandchildren's apprenticeships if they want them.
S4.feel: Uneasy for the village and grandchildren, not for herself.
S4.quote: No one on the roofs, no one in the milking parlours.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, her personal plan holds, but her worry moves to her valley emptying out. She'd pick up more AI once others had. Supporting apprenticeships is her way of acting on her beliefs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Karl and I both out, two months saved, and nowhere in the valley to go. What would help is apprenticeships for the new kind of work, even for older people, and something to keep small rural firms going, so the villages don't empty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether it's different out in the country. In town, if one firm shuts, there's another down the road. Out here, if Hollins shuts, I'd be driving forty minutes for any job at all.

headlineQuote: Out here, if Hollins shuts, I'd be driving forty minutes for any job at all.
portrait: Carla is a fifty-eight-year-old former dairy farmer who started roofing as a labourer after the family sold their herd to clear debts. She's rooted in church, family and village life, supports apprenticeships over handouts, and uses AI now and then, mostly for recipes. Steady change leaves her uneasy because rural building jobs are few. Two-year AGI alarms her because her husband's tanker driving would go too and their savings are thin, while five years lets her fall back on hens, land rent and early retirement, and ten years turns her worry to the village and her son in banking.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Karl would both lose work with two months saved and few jobs in the valley.
whatWouldHelp: Apprenticeships for new kinds of work, even for older people, and support to keep small rural firms going.
